Command Descriptions

The following command descriptions are listed as the command name plus the <color:keyword>underlying command key. This is followed by the command name and <color:keyword>roguelike keyset key, if different from the underlying command key. Then comes a brief description of the command, including information about alternative methods of specifying the command in each keyset, when needed.

Several commands (tunnel, disarm, bash, open) are automatically repeated as many times as necessary (up to the current <color:keyword>retry_obvious_count setting, which defaults to 100) if no specific repeat count is given and the option has not been turned off. Some other commands allow using repeat counts as arguments; for example, commands which need a quantity can use the repeat count instead of asking for a quantity, allowing the use of <color:keypress>0d to drop all. Commands which ask for a quantity will convert any letters into the maximal legal value.

Press <color:keypress>? for commands to use within the help system.

Inventory Commands

Inventory List (<color:keypress>i)

Displays a list of objects being carried but not equipped. You have up to 26 slots in your inventory, not counting equipment slots. Identical objects can often form a "stack" which only occupies a single slot, like the 4 torches, 26 arrows and 13 rations of food in the sample below; stacks have a maximum size of 99 objects.

Inventory | Equipment

a) , 13 Rations of Food 13.0 lb

b) - a Wand {tried} 0.2 lb

c) ~ 4 Wooden Torches (with 2000 turns of light) 12.0 lb

d) ( a Filthy Rag 2.0 lb

e) ) a Small Leather Shield {average} 5.0 lb

f) ) a Small Leather Shield 5.0 lb

g) | a Main Gauche {average} 3.0 lb

h) { 26 Arrows (3d4) (+0,+0)

45.4 lb

Carrying 93.4 pounds (71% capacity).

You can press <color:keypress>/ here to toggle between the inventory list, the equipment list and potentially other item inventories like your quiver.

Equipment List (<color:keypress>e)

Use this command to display a list of the objects currently worn or wielded by your character. Your character typically has 13 slots for equipment, each corresponding to a different location on the body; each slot may contain only a single object at a time, and each slot may only contain objects of the proper type. Note that some races (and most monster forms) have body types that differ from the typical humanoid, so the number and types of your equipment slots can vary. Here is a sample equipment list from a human warrior:

a) | Right Hand: a Broad Sword (2d6) (+0,+0) 15.0 lb

b) ) Left Hand : a Small Leather Shield [3,+0] 5.0 lb

c) } Shooting : a Short Bow (x2.50) (+0,+0) 3.0 lb

d) Quiver :

e) Right Ring:

f) Left Ring :

g) Neck :

h) ~ Light : a Wooden Torch (with 1983 turns of ligh 3.0 lb

i) [ Body : Chain Mail (-2) [14,+0] 22.0 lb

j) Cloak :

k) Head :

l) Hands :

m) Feet :

48.0 lb

Each slot has a descriptive label (like "Right Hand") that determines what type of object it may receive; the right hand and left hand, for example, accept weapons and shields. And yes, you can wield two weapons, or two shields! The slots for most items are very intuitive (gloves go on your hands, helmets go on your head), but some might be a bit surprising, like harps going into the Shooting slot.

Inspect Item (<color:keypress>I)

This command lets you examine an item in detail, listing whatever special powers of the object you have identified, mentioning if the object still has hidden powers, and noting the item's weight and estimated value. Here too, use <color:keypress>/ to toggle between your pack, equipment, and other relevant inventories. This is an especially handy command for artifacts and ego-items.

Get Objects (<color:keypress>g)

This command will get any objects located on the same tile as the player (Mogaminator applies). As a convenience, picking up items does not consume time.

Auto-Get Objects (<color:keypress>^G)

This command will get any objects located on the same tile as the player (Mogaminator applies). In addition, this command will automatically travel to and get other objects in line of sight. With <color:keyword>auto_get_objects enabled, any object registered for either auto-pickup or auto-destroy will qualify for automatic get. If that is too much for you (maybe you enjoy cleaning up after battles?), the <color:keyword>auto_get_ammo option only applies to objects inscribed with <color:keypress>=g; which is typically your ammo, or perhaps spikes on a ninja.

The auto-get travels will terminate when there are no more visible qualifying objects; if your pack becomes full; or if you are disturbed for any reason, such as a nasty dragon waking up and deciding to breathe on you. Auto-get is both safer and more limited than travelling through the object list; auto-get usually only cleans up a single room since the objects must be visible to qualify, while the object list and the <color:keypress>H/<color:keypress>^E command allow lengthy automatic travels, potentially into harm's way (although these journeys also stop if bad things happen).

Drop Item (<color:keypress>d)

This drops an item from your inventory or equipment onto the dungeon floor. If the floor spot you are standing on already has an object in it, or rejects object drops altogether (doors, stairs, traps, some terrain types like deep lava), the game will attempt to drop the item onto an adjacent space. If nothing else works, the item will be dropped onto a square that already has an object in it; but be warned that if there simply are no acceptable squares nearby the object may disappear entirely. If the pile selected for dropping contains multiple items, you may specify a quantity.

Destroy Item (<color:keypress>k) or (<color:keypress>^D)

This destroys an item in your inventory or on the dungeon floor. If the selected pile contains multiple objects, you may specify a quantity. You must always verify this command, except in the case of worthless junk items.

Wear/Wield Equipment (<color:keypress>w)

To wear or wield an object, use this command. Since only one object can be in each equipment slot at a time, if you wear or wield an item into a slot which is already occupied, the old item will first be taken off, and may be dropped if there is no room for it in your inventory.

Take Off Equipment (<color:keypress>t) or (<color:keypress>T)

Use this command to take off a piece of equipment and return it to your inventory. If there is no room in your inventory for the item, your pack will overflow and you will drop the item after taking it off. Occasionally, you will run into a cursed item which cannot be removed; these items normally penalize you in some way, and can only be taken off after the curse has been removed.

Movement Commands

Walk (with pickup) (<color:keypress>;)

Moves one step in the given direction. The square you are moving into must not be blocked by walls or doors. You will pick up any items in the destination grid if the <color:keyword>always_pickup option is set. This command can take a count and requires a direction. You may also use the "original" direction keys (both keysets) or the "roguelike" direction keys (roguelike keyset) to walk in a direction (they are keymapped to this command). If the Mogaminator or the easy auto-destroyer is active, specified objects will be picked up or destroyed.

Walk (flip pickup) (<color:keypress>-)

This is just like normal move, except that the "Pick things up" option is inverted. In other words, you will pick things up if and only if <color:keyword>always_pickup is <color:keyword>not set. This command can take a count and requires a direction. If the Mogaminator or the easy auto-destroyer is active, specified objects will be picked up or destroyed.

This is also the command for deliberately walking into a trap.

Run (<color:keypress>.) or (<color:keypress>,)

This command will move in the given direction, following any bends in the corridor, until you either have to make a "choice" between two directions or you are disturbed. You can configure what will disturb you by setting the disturbance options. Run requires a direction. By default <color:keypress>Shift+DIR is keymapped to <color:keypress>.DIR, although with the original keyset this may run into technical limitations on some platforms. If the Mogaminator or the easy auto-destroyer is active, specified objects will be picked up or destroyed.

Go Up Staircase (<color:keypress><)

Climbs up if you are standing on an up staircase or shaft. In the wilderness, opens the global map for viewing; you can look around freely, but travel is blocked while alert monsters are nearby.

Unless you are playing in <color:keyword>coffee-break mode or have activated the ironman_downward option, there is always at least one up staircase on every level. Going up a staircase will take you to either the surface or a new dungeon level. Note that levels are semi-persistent; they can be returned to while you remain in the dungeon (supposing up staircases exist), but are lost forever when you return to surface.

Go Down Staircase (<color:keypress>>)

Descends if you are standing on a down staircase or shaft. In the wilderness, returns from global map to local map.

There are always at least two staircases going down on each level, except for quest levels (which have none until the quest monster is killed) and the bottom levels of dungeons. Going down a staircase will take you to a new dungeon level (see "Go Up Staircase" for notes).

Travel to Nearest Interesting Item (<color:keypress>H or <color:keypress>^E)

Locates and automatically travels to the nearest known item that is unidentified, either has not been pseudo-ID'd or has been sensed as an artifact or ego item, is not considered unworthy of picking up by an active Mogaminator, and to which a known route has been mapped. Convenient for quickly locating items you forgot to pick up or identify after you have otherwise a dungeon level, or after killing a high-level monster who dropped loot all over the place.

Resume Journey (<color:keypress>J) or Resume Travelling (<color:keypress>()

Resumes a previous travel that was interrupted before reaching its target. This command can also be used in the monster and object lists to start a new travel; for this purpose, the <color:keypress>J key is also used by the roguelike keyset.

Resting Commands

Stay Still (with pickup) (<color:keypress>,) or (<color:keypress>.)

Stays in the same square for one move. If you normally pick up objects you encounter, you will pick up whatever you are standing on. This command can take a count. You may also use the "5" key (both keysets). If the Mogaminator or the easy auto-destroyer is active, specified objects will be picked up or destroyed.

Rest (<color:keypress>R)

Resting is better for you than repeatedly staying still, and can be told to automatically stop after a certain amount of time, or when various conditions are met. In any case, you always wake up when anything disturbing happens, or when you press any key. This command requests a count if no count is specified; the count defaults to the special value <color:keypress>&, which means "rest until fully healed and no longer gorged". Another special value, <color:keypress>* for "rest to full HP/SP", is also accepted.

Searching Commands

Search (<color:keypress>s)

This command can be used to locate hidden traps and secret doors in the spaces adjacent to the player. More than a single turn of searching will be required in most cases. You should always search a chest before trying to open it, since they are generally trapped; though if nothing appears, you may have found a rare trapless chest. This command can take a count, which is useful if you are fairly sure of finding something eventually, since the command stops as soon as anything is found.

Toggle Search Mode (<color:keypress>S) or (<color:keypress>#)

This command will take you into and out of search mode. When first pressed, the message "Searching" will appear at the bottom of the screen. You are now taking two turns for each command, one for the command and one turn to search. This means that you are taking twice the time to move around the dungeon, and therefore twice the food. Search mode will automatically turn off if you are disturbed. You may also turn off search mode by entering the Search Mode command again.

Alter Commands

Tunnel (<color:keypress>T) or (<color:keypress>^T)

Tunneling or mining is a very useful art. There are many kinds of rock, with varying hardness, including:

<$:FF_PERMANENT> Permanent Rock Permanent

<$:FF_GRANITE> Granite Very Hard

<$:FF_QUARTZ_VEIN> Quartz Veins Hard

<$:FF_MAGMA_VEIN> Magma veins Soft

<$:FF_RUBBLE> Rubble Very Soft

Quartz and Magma veins may sometimes contain treasure; known treasures will be displayed as <$:FF_MAGMA_TREASURE>, but not all treasures are visible without detection. Rubble sometimes covers an object. Tunneling is difficult unless you are wielding a heavy weapon or a digging implement or your Strength is very high. This command can take a count, requires a direction, and is affected by the <color:keyword>retry_obvious_count option.

Open a Door or Chest (<color:keypress>o)

To open a chest, you must use this command (for doors, simply walking into a closed door automatically attempts to open it). If the door or chest is locked, you will attempt to pick the lock based on your disarming ability; if you open a trapped chest without disarming the traps first, the traps will be set off. You may need several tries to open a door or chest, and rarely doors will be jammed shut and need to be bashed open. Open can take a count, requires a direction, and is affected by the <color:keyword>retry_obvious_count option.

Close a Door (<color:keypress>c)

Non-intelligent and some other creatures cannot open doors, so shutting doors can be quite valuable. Broken doors cannot be closed. Bashing a door open may break it. Close can take a count, requires a direction, and is affected by the <color:keyword>retry_obvious_count option.

Jam a Door / Shortcut Move (<color:keypress>j) or (<color:keypress>S)

Many monsters can simply open closed doors, and can eventually get through a locked door. You may therefore occasionally want to jam a door shut with iron spikes. Each spike used on the door will make it harder to bash down the door, up to a certain limit. Smaller monsters are less able to bash down doors. In order to use this command, you must be carrying iron spikes. Jam or Spike requires a direction.

Bash a Door (<color:keypress>B) or Force a Door (<color:keypress>f)

This command allows you to bash down jammed doors. Your bashing ability increases with strength. Bashing open a door can (briefly) throw you off balance. Doors that are stuck, or which have been jammed closed with spikes can only be opened by bashing, and all closed doors can be bashed open if desired. Bashing a door open may permanently break it. Bash/Force can take a count, requires a direction, and is affected by the <color:keyword>retry_obvious_count option.

Disarm a Trap or Chest (<color:keypress>D)

You can attempt to disarm traps on the floor or on chests. If you fail, there is a chance that you will blunder and set it off. You can only disarm a trap after you have found it (with the Search command, by detection, or by previously triggering it). Disarm can take a count, requires a direction, and is affected by the <color:keyword>retry_obvious_count option. Walking into known floor traps automatically attempts to disarm them unless the <color:keyword>easy_disarm option has been disabled; use <color:keypress>- if you wish to deliberately walk into a trap without disarming it.

Alter Adjacent Grid (<color:keypress>+)

This all-purpose super-command allows the use of a single keypress to select any of the "obvious" commands above (attack, tunnel, bash, open, disarm, close). <color:keypress>Ctrl-[dir] is by default macroed to be equivalent to alter-[dir], in both keysets. Alter can take a count, requires a direction, and is affected by the <color:keyword>retry_obvious_count option.

Spell and Prayer Commands

Browse Magic List (<color:keypress>b) or Peruse Magic List (<color:keypress>P)

All characters which can cast spells can use this command. When this command is used, all of the spells available to you (or contained in a selected magic book) are displayed, along with such information as their level, the amount of mana required to cast them, and whether or not you know the spell. And when you select a spell from the list, a short description of the selected spell's effect will be displayed.

Gain New Spells or Prayers (<color:keypress>G)

Use this command to actually learn new spells or prayers. When you are able to learn new spells or prayers, the word Study will appear in the status area of the screen. If you have a book in your possession, containing spells or prayers which you may learn, then you may choose to study that book. If you are a Priest, Paladin, Ranger, Monk or Force-Trainer, your gods will choose a prayer for you; other classes can choose which spell they wish to study, and even study the same spell a second time. There are four books in each realm, some normally found only in the dungeon.

Use a Magic Spell/Mental Power (<color:keypress>m)

To use a book spell (or prayer), you must have previously learned the spell and must have in your inventory a book from which the spell can be read. Each spell has a chance of failure which starts out fairly large but decreases as you gain levels. If you don't have enough mana to cast a spell, you will be prompted for confirmation. If you decide to go ahead, the chance of failure is greatly increased, and you may lose a point of constitution. Since you must read the spell from a book, you cannot be blind or confused while casting, and there must be some light present.

For classes who do not learn book spells but do learn magic or mental powers through other means (commonly just by leveling up), this command may obey slightly different rules. For most (but not all) classes, this command will not work at all if your character is Mundane or has equipped an Anti-Magic item.

Use Bonus Power (<color:keypress>U) or (<color:keypress>O)

Some races and classes have special natural abilities. For example, a Cyclops may <color:keyword>Throw Boulders and a Gnome may <color:keyword>Blink away from danger. A Warrior can learn the power of <color:keyword>Sword Dancing. Also, it is possible to become mutated and gain a power, such as the ability to shoot <color:keyword>Laser Beams from your eyes! If you have no special powers, this command will not do anything.

Object Use Commands

Eat Food (<color:keypress>E)

You must eat regularly to prevent starvation. As you grow hungry, a message will appear in the status portion of the screen saying Hungry. If you go hungry long enough, you will become Weak, then start Fainting, and eventually starve to death. Use this command to eat food from your inventory - though it is also possible to eat straight from the floor...

Fuel Lantern/Torch (<color:keypress>F)

If you are using a torch and have more torches in your pack, or you are using a lantern and have flasks of oil in your pack, you can refuel your light source with this command. Torches and Lanterns have limited fuel capacity; in general, two flasks will fully fuel a lantern and two torches will fully fuel a torch.

Quaff Potion (<color:keypress>q)

Use this command to drink a potion, fully consuming it unless you are a Potion-speciality Devicemaster. The effects could be good or bad, depending on the potion.

Read Scroll (<color:keypress>r)

Use this command to read a magic scroll. Reading a scroll causes the parchment to disintegrate as the magic takes effect. Most scrolls which prompt for more information can be aborted (by pressing <color:keypress>ESC) without consuming the scroll. Note that magic is fickle, and the scroll must be read with care; mispronounce the incantations, and nothing happens.

Activate Item (<color:keypress>A)

You have heard rumors of special items deep in the dungeon that let you breathe fire like a dragon or illuminate rooms with just a thought. Should you ever be lucky enough to find such an item, this command will let you activate its special ability. Only equipped items can be activated, and they usually take a certain amount of time to <color:keyword>recharge before you can activate them again. Activations resemble scroll, wand, staff and rod effects: all require Magic Device Skill and have a chance to fail.

Aim Wand (<color:keypress>a) or Zap Wand (<color:keypress>z)

This command attempts to use a wand. Wand effects are normally bolts, beams, balls or breaths, and so need to be aimed; accordingly, this command requires a direction and can use a target.

Use Staff (<color:keypress>u) or Zap Staff (<color:keypress>Z)

This command attempts to use a staff. Staves normally either have an area effect or affect a specific object, and therefore do not need to be aimed.

Zap Rod (<color:keypress>z) or Activate Rod (<color:keypress>a)

This command attempts to use a rod; rods can have either staff-like or wand-like effects. This command may require a direction (depending on the type of rod, and whether you are aware of its type) and can use a target.

Edit an item inscription (<color:keypress>Z) or (<color:keypress>{)

This command adds, changes, or clears an inscription on an object. The inscription is displayed inside curly braces after the object description. The inscription is limited to the particular object (or pile) and is not automatically transferred to all similar objects. Certain inscriptions give the game instructions for how to handle or label the item; see for more information. Leaving the inscription blank clears it.

Dungeon notes (<color:keypress>})

This command opens a notes menu for save-wide, dungeon, floor, or building reminders. Notes are saved per character, can be reviewed from the menu, and matching notes are shown automatically when you return to their location.

Throwing and Missile Weapons

Fire Item (<color:keypress>f) or (<color:keypress>t)

Fires a selected projectile suitable for your current ranged weapon, provided that you have a ranged weapon equipped. Slings only shoot pebbles and iron shots; bows only shoot arrows; and crossbows only shoot bolts. Projectiles are typically fired from your quiver, but can also be shot directly from your inventory or even from the floor. This command requires a direction, and can take a target.

Throw Item (<color:keypress>v)

You may throw any object carried by your character. The lighter the object, the farther you can throw it. Only one object from a stack may be thrown at a time. Thrown objects may or may not damage monsters. Throwing an object can break it. Throwing a potion at a wall always breaks it, potentially causing splash damage. This command requires a direction, and can take a target.

Set Target (*)

This command allows you to aim your spells, arrows and such at a specific monster or grid, even if they are not in one of the eight compass directions; it works both inside and outside direction prompts. This command can also be used as a substitute for the <color:keypress>look command, which is especially convenient if what you wish to look at is a monster.

The targeting prompt offers many options. The first target offered will be the nearest monster in line of sight, with other monsters in line of sight as alternative targets. Use direction keys to cycle between monsters; <color:keypress>+ and <color:keypress>- also work, but are less intuitive.

If you wish to target (or inspect) a square with no monster on it, press <color:keypress>p or <color:keypress>o, switching to a mode where direction keys simply move the cursor. (This mode is automatically entered if no hostile monsters are in line of sight. <color:keypress>o and <color:keypress>p are identical except in one respect: pressing <color:keypress>p moves the cursor to your own location.) At any time, press <color:keypress>5, <color:keypress>t or <color:keypress>. to accept the current target, <color:keypress>q or <color:keypress>ESC to exit targeting mode, <color:keypress>r to recall lore about a currently targeted monster, <color:keypress>x to see all items on the target square, and <color:keypress>J/<color:keypress>( to select a square as a travel target. See for more detail.

Note that when you cast a spell or fire an object at a target location, the path chosen is the <color:keyword>direct path towards that location, which may or may not be the path you want. Sometimes, by clever choice of a side location as your target, you may be able to aim at squares not directly in line of sight:

Position: an unknown grid [q,t,p,m,x,j,+,-,?,<dir>]

##........#.... #%%####

#........\...... #

%.......}{\@.... #

%#%..........*.... #

## ........*... ... #

# ......*... .d. #

# ..(.#*. .#####

# .##* T #

# ^ #####* ##########

## # #* '

# # ##* ############

# # #* ###

# # ##* ##

## # # * #

# # ##* #

######### #*#########

Notice that bright-red *? There's a dragon on that square I cannot target directly; but I managed to include that square in my spell's path by using <color:keypress>p to target a location on the southern edge of the map.

Note that bolt spells always stop at the first monster in the spell's path, but beam and breath spells affect all squares, and ball spells can reach the target square by flying over monsters' heads if necessary. If the <color:keypress>* command is used on the overworld map, it hooks into the similar <color:keypress>look command. Using the <color:keypress>* command consumes no time.

Looking Commands

Display Monster List (<color:keypress>Y) or (<color:keypress>[)

This command displays a list of all monsters currently visible. This is a quick way to tell if there are any uniques or other threatening monsters nearby, and is most commonly used immediately after a summon or detection.

Display Object List (<color:keypress>])

This command displays a list of all known objects on the level, as well as other interesting nearby features such as shops or dungeon entrances. Pressing <color:keypress>S with the object list active toggles whether stairs are included in the object list. The object list is a handy way to locate stairs, artifacts, unidentified items and other targets of interest on the level, and makes it possible to travel to such targets directly by scrolling down to the target and pressing <color:keypress>J.

Full Screen Map (<color:keypress>M)

This command will show a map of the entire dungeon, scaled to fit on a single screen. Only the major dungeon features will be visible because of the scale, so even some important objects may not show up on the map. This is particularly useful for quickly identifying unexplored areas of the dungeon or determining your location relative to the dungeon's edges. This command takes no time.

  +------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |                          ######  #########                       |
  |                   ########....####.......%                       |
  |             ######......#####.####.......#                       |
  |             d......##            ######%%#                       |
  |            <###.....#                                            |
  |             ##'.....#                                            |
  |             ##'.....#                                            |
  |              ##+#####                                            |
  |     #####    ..                                                  |
  |     #...#    ##                                                  |
  |     ###%'##%#%#                                                  |
  |        %###%%<#                                                  |
  |              .#                                                  |
  |              %#                                                  |
  |              %%                                                  |
  |            #%#%%                                                 |
  |            #...#                                                 |
  |            ###%#                                                 |

If the Mogaminator is active, specified objects can be displayed on this map; this is an obsolete functionality, though, as it is always more convenient to just use the <color:keypress>] object list.

Locate Player on Map (<color:keypress>L) or Where is the Player? (<color:keypress>W)

This command lets you scroll your map around, looking at all sectors of the current dungeon level, until you press escape, at which point the map will be re-centered on the player if necessary. To scroll the map around, simply press any of the "direction" keys. The top line will display the sector location, and the offset from your current sector. This command takes no time.

Recenter Viewport (<color:keypress>^V)

This command re-centers the viewport on the player; the game does automatically adjust the viewport as you move, but only when you approach the edge. This command is a quicker alternative to the Locate Player on Map command just discussed, though some players go a step further and activate the <color:keyword>center_player option ().

Look Around (<color:keypress>l) or Examine Things (<color:keypress>x)

This command is used to look around at nearby monsters (to determine their type and health) and objects (to determine their type). It is also used to find out what objects (if any) are under monsters, and if a monster is currently inside a wall. This command takes no time.

This command is very closely related to the <color:keypress>* targeting command, and most of the targeting prompt's special keys also work in the look prompt. It is often convenient to use <color:keypress>* instead of this command, especially if you wish to look at a monster; on the other hand, <color:keypress>l/<color:keypress>x is better for inspecting town buildings.

Message Commands

Repeat Level Feeling (<color:keypress>^F)

Repeats the current feeling about the dungeon level.

View Previous Messages (<color:keypress>^P)

This command shows you all the recent messages. You can scroll through them, or exit with ESCAPE. This command takes no time.

Take notes (<color:keypress>:)

This command allows you to take notes, which will then appear in your message list (prefixed with "Note:"). This command takes no time. It also adds a tiny screenshot to your message log. For example:

  Note: These bats are so dead!!
              #.################.#
              #..........<.......#
              #.##############>#.#
          #####.#              #.######
          #.....#              #.......
          #.#####              ########
          #.#                         #
  #########'########
  #................#
  #...........@....#
  #.......b........#
  #................#
  #.........b......'
  #................#
  #................#
  #................#
  #................#
  ##################

Targetting a Fruit bat.
The Fruit bat dies.

Targetting a Fruit bat.
The Fruit bat dies.

Game Status Commands

Character Sheet (<color:keypress>C)

Brings up a full description of your character, including your resistances, skill levels, current and potential stats, equipment, inventory, home inventory, average damage in melee and ranged combat, spell repertoire, quest history, and other information. From this screen, you can use the <color:keypress>| command to create a character dump.

Character Sheet Snapshot Compare

Within the Character Sheet, you may save and compare full sheet snapshots without leaving the screen. Press <color:keypress>c to save the currently displayed sheet, or <color:keypress>C to compare against the default saved snapshot if one exists. For full command details, including extra snapshot slots and shifted-symbol direct-load aliases, see .

Knowledge Menu (<color:keypress>~)

The command opens a menu from which you can select or recall information about your character, artifacts, monsters, identified objects, etc.:

Object Knowledge Dungeon Knowledge

(a) Artifacts (d) Dungeons

(o) Objects (q) Quests

(e) Egos (t) Terrain Symbols

(_) Auto Pick/Destroy

Self Knowledge

Monster Knowledge (@) About Yourself

(m) Known Monsters (W) Weapon Damage

(w) Wanted Monsters (H) High Score List

(u) Remaining Uniques

(k) Kill Count Skills

(p) Pets (P) Proficiency

(s) Spell Proficiency

As you can see, there is a lot of information here; poke around and you will see what's available.

Display game time (<color:keypress>^T) or (<color:keypress>')

This command shows you current date and time in the game, usually with a short comment. (The basic information, without the comments, is also available through the <color:keypress>C character sheet.)

Saving and Exiting Commands

Save and Quit (<color:keypress>^X)

To save your game so that you can return to it later, use this command. Save files will also be generated (hopefully) if the game crashes due to a system error. After you die, you can use your savefile to play again with the same options and lore.

Save (<color:keypress>^S)

This command saves the game but doesn't exit. Use this frequently if you are paranoid about having the computer crash while you are playing.

Quit (commit suicide) (<color:keypress>Q)

Kills your character and exits the game. You will be prompted to make sure you really want to do this, and then asked to verify that choice. Note that dead characters are dead forever.

User Preference Commands

See for a description of the user preference commands together with a detailed description of this function.

Interact with Options (<color:keypress>=)

Allosw you to interact with options. Note that using the cheat options may mark your savefile as unsuitable for the high score list.

Interact with Macros (<color:keypress>@)

Allows you to interact with macros. You may load or save macros from user pref files, create macros of various types, or define keymaps.

Interact with Visuals (<color:keypress>%)

Allows you to interact with visuals. You may load or save visuals from user pref files, or modify the attr/char mappings for the monsters, objects, and terrain features.

Interact with Colors (<color:keypress>&)

Allows the user to interact with colors. This command only works on some systems.

Reload Mogaminator Preferences (<color:keypress>$)

This command will reload "pickpref.prf" and "pickpref-<<playername>>.prf" for the Mogaminator; only needs to be used if you have edited these files during the game with an external text editor.

Edit Mogaminator Preferences (<color:keypress>_)

Prompts before opening the pickup-preference editor, and can activate the Mogaminator if it was not yet active. The <color:keypress>ESC key will open the menu in this editor, including an option to disable the Mogaminator and exit. Press <color:keypress>^Q or <color:keypress>^W to quit the editor.

Help

Help (<color:keypress>?)

Brings up the online help system. In some situations (like within the help itself) it may bring up a specific help page.

Identify Symbol (<color:keypress>/)

Use this command to find out what a character stands for; for instance, by pressing <color:keypress>/. you can find out that the <color:keypress>. symbol stands for a floor spot. Note that if you wish to see information about a specific monster nearby, you should use the <color:keypress>* command instead of this command.

If you do use Identify Symbol on a monster symbol, you will be reminded of the species corresponding to the symbol and get a list of all monsters of that species that you have seen. Similar information is available through the <color:keypress>~ Knowledge Menu.

There are four special commands you can use with Identify Symbol: <color:keypress>Ctrl-A to recall all known monsters, <color:keypress>Ctrl-U to recall all known uniques, <color:keypress>Ctrl-N to recall all known non-uniques and <color:keypress>Ctrl-M to recall all known monsters matching a string you type. Press <color:keypress>k to sort these lists by number of kills, <color:keypress>p to sort them by the native depths of the monsters and <color:keypress>ESC to exit.

Game Version (<color:keypress>V)

This command will tell you what version of the game you are using, as well as the current size of the map. For more information, see .

Extra Commands

Repeat Last Command (<color:keypress>n) or (<color:keypress>X)

This command repeats the previously executed command with all its arguments. Very useful for repeatedly firing at or casting the same spell at a given enemy.

Record Command (<color:keypress>")

Commands that you enter may be recorded to any normal ASCII character register. In fact, every command that you manually enter is automatically recorded to the <color:keypress>. register. When you repeat the last command, you are really playing back the contents of this special <color:keypress>. register. But you can also record the next command to a register of your choosing and then play it back manually later; for example, the command sequence <color:keypress>"Fmae*t records the command <color:keypress>mae*t to the <color:keypress>F register in addition to the <color:keypress>. register. You can later play back this command with <color:keypress>'F whereas playing back with <color:keypress>'. or <color:keypress>n is only valid on the very next turn.

Playback Command (<color:keypress>')

As mentioned above, you may record commands with the <color:keypress>" command and play them back later with the <color:keypress>' command. Commands are stored in registers, each of which is addressed with a single ASCII character. For example, if you record a command with <color:keypress>"t<cmd>, then you may later play it back by pressing <color:keypress>'t. These command registers are temporary and will be erased every time you restart the game. To view your recorded commands, choose the <color:keypress>' register (i.e., press <color:keypress>'' from the top level). You can then enter the register you wish to use (e.g. <color:keypress>''t works the same as <color:keypress>'t except that the register contents of all recorded commands are displayed to you after you press the second <color:keypress>').

The playback command is rarely used, as macros and keymaps () are usually preferable.

Toggle Choice Window (<color:keypress>^I)

Toggles subwindow display between your inventory and your equipment. This command only applies if you have an inventory/equipment subwindow.

Redraw Screen (<color:keypress>^R)

This command adapts to various changes in global options, and redraws all of the windows. It is polite to use this command if somebody starts watching your game when you play on <color:keyword>angband.live; also use this command if you feel there are graphical errors or the game has not properly responded to visual changes you made. When in doubt, use it.

Create screen dump (<color:keypress>))

This command creates a document of the current screen and then displays that document to you in the game's internal file viewer. You may then save the document as either plaintext or as html, using the <color:keypress>| command. To create an html file, simply give the file an html extension. Note that if you are playing with graphics enabled, then this command will attempt to convert to normal textual display before creating the screen dump.

Command your pets (<color:keypress>p)

If you have pets, use this command to give orders or toggle pet options. See for details.

Home, Sweet Home

Press for the &lt;color:keyword&gt;Quick Reference.

Your home is a special building found in all the normal towns on the surface (Outpost, Morivant, Anambar, Thalos, Telmora and Angwil). In your home, you may stash goodies for future use; there are no limits on the amount of objects you may store in your home, but if your house gets too cluttered, finding the item you are looking for can be a chore. Somehow, magically, all of your homes share the same inventory.

Using Your Home

When you first enter your home, you will see an empty inventory. To leave items at your home, simply drop them using the <color:keypress>d command and select the item you wish to drop. Similarly, to get items from your home, use the <color:keypress>g command and then enter the label of the item you want. After a bit of play, your home might look like this:

Once there are more objects than can be displayed on your screen, the inventory will be listed in pages. Use the <color:keypress>Page Up and <color:keypress>Page Down keys to navigate.

If you find your home too cluttered, you may want to clean up a bit. The simple solution is to <color:keypress>get items into your pack, walk outside, and drop them on the town commons; but this is littering, and also a bit of work. There's an alternative way to clean up, with the <color:keypress>r command; be careful, though, since using it permanently destroys the selected items, you are not allowed to specify a quantity, and you will stay in item-removal mode until you press <color:keypress>ESC.

Note that you can view your home inventory not just at your home, but also through your Character Sheet (<color:keypress>C); although you cannot select (or inspect) individual items this way, it is often the fastest and most convenient way to locate useful items hidden in pages of trash, especially if you are shuffling your equipment. This reduces the need to clean up.

The Museum

The Museum behaves very much like your home, except that you cannot take items from the Museum: all donations to the Museum are final. The Museum is exclusively for keepsakes - which some players seem to have awfully many of!

Another difference between the Museum and your home is that items given to the Museum are automatically *Identified*, as with shops; but there is no advantage to *identifying* items through the Museum compared to doing so through a shop, where you get paid for the item and can potentially buy it back.

Quick Reference

Basic Commands

<color:keypress>d s Drop an item from your pack to your home

<color:keypress>g p b Get an item from your home to your pack

<color:keypress>x Examine an item in your home

<color:keypress>r Permanently remove items from your home

<color:keypress>q Esc Leave your home

Extra Commands

<color:keypress>w Wear an item

<color:keypress>t T Take off an item

<color:keypress>k ^D Destroy items in your pack

<color:keypress>e Display equipment

<color:keypress>i Display inventory

<color:keypress>I Inspect objects in your pack

<color:keypress>Tab Toggle inventory/equipment subwindows

<color:keypress>{ Edit item inscriptions in your pack

<color:keypress>} Open the dungeon notes menu

<color:keypress>C Display character sheet

Note: These <color:keyword>Extra Commands are simply normal game commands made available for your convenience so you need not leave your home to use them. However, the keybindings for these commands are <color:keyword>hard-coded, so any keymaps you may have defined will not apply.

Navigation

<color:keypress>Page Up Scroll through long object lists

<color:keypress>Page Down

<color:keypress>Space Same as Page Down

<color:keypress>- Same as Page Up

Display Options

<color:keypress>^W Toggle weights (see )

<color:keypress>^G Toggle graphics (see )

The Monster List

This command lists all monsters you are currently aware of. Depending on your list-display options, it can split line-of-sight monsters into a top section, push awake monsters ahead of sleeping ones, and sort by either monster level or distance. When grouping stays enabled, monsters of the same apparent race are still grouped together, except that awake-first sorting splits mixed awake/asleep rows.

Quick Summary

<color:keypress>Up/Down Scroll One Line at a Time

<color:keypress>PageUp/PageDown Scroll One Page at a Time

<color:keypress>Home/End Scroll to Top/Bottom of List

<color:keypress>/ or R Recall Selected Monster

<color:keypress>P Probe Selected Monster (if allowed)

<color:keypress>N Name Selected Pet (if allowed)

<color:keypress>` or J Travel to Selected Monster

<color:keypress>* or T or 5 Target Selected Monster

<color:keypress>+/- Adjust List Width

<color:keypress>ESC or Q Quit this Command

<color:keypress>? Display this Help Topic

<color:keypress>[a-z] Select next matching entry

Note: Since lowercase keystrokes attempt to match the next entry, only uppercase alphabetic commands are available. For example, to recall monster info, you must press <color:keypress>R rather than the usual <color:keypress>r. The exception is that for users of the roguelike keyset, the usual up/down commands <color:keypress>k and <color:keypress>j will scroll up and down, even at the cost of not matching an entry.

Note: If <color:keyword>quick_messages is enabled, then an unhandled keystroke will dismiss the monster list.

The Dreaded -more- Prompt

Note: If you are viewing this, it is because you pressed <color:keypress>? when prompted for -more- messages.

In the bad old days, when there was only one message line, -more- prompts were very frequent and this file was 40 times longer, detailing all the cute keys and options for reducing the number of -more- prompts you would get. The cute keys still exist, like <color:keypress>n to dismiss all messages up to the next message boundary and <color:keypress>ESC to dismiss all messages, period; but in practice things are very simple now. Press <color:keypress>SPACE or <color:keypress>ENTER every time you receive a -more- prompt, and you can't go wrong!

Selecting Objects

Objects are a big part of playing <color:keyword>FrogComposband. Many commands (such as quaffing potions or reading scrolls) require you to select an object to use. Other commands allow you to view and inspect the objects you are carrying or using. This helpfile explains the user interface for viewing and selecting objects.

To choose an object, simply press the indicated letter. What happens next depends on the context of the object prompt and is indicated by the bottom line on the dialog. In this case, you are simply browsing your gear, so what could be more useful than letting you inspect individual objects?

You'll notice that selecting an object in this case did not dismiss the dialog. This is both unusual and useful, since you might want to inspect multiple objects before you are done. A few other game commands behave this way, such as Inscribing (<color:keypress>{) objects, but most dialogs are dismissed after a selection is made.

The Object List

This command displays all known objects on the current level. Objects the <color:keyword>Mogaminator would like to pick up are shown near the top in the <color:keyword>wanted objects category, while everything else is shown below in the <color:keyword>other objects category. Objects in both groups are sorted by their estimated value; the location of each object, relative to your current position, is indicated with directions as in <color:keyword>N 23 E 11. The object list also displays dungeon entrances, quest entrances and town shops, and the inclusion of staircases in the list can be toggled.

Quick Summary

<color:keypress>Up/Down Scroll One Line at a Time

<color:keypress>PageUp/PageDown Scroll One Page at a Time

<color:keypress>Home/End Scroll to Top/Bottom of List

<color:keypress>/ or I Inspect Selected Object

<color:keypress>J or ` or ( Travel to Selected Object

<color:keypress>+/- Adjust List Width

<color:keypress>A Toggle Ammo

<color:keypress>D Toggle Identified Items

<color:keypress>E Toggle Sensed Items

<color:keypress>N Toggle Unsensed Items

<color:keypress>S Toggle Inclusion of Stairs

<color:keypress>U Toggle Mogaminator Ignored/Destroyed Items

<color:keypress>ESC or Q Quit this Command

<color:keypress>? Display this Help Topic

<color:keypress>[a-z] Select next matching entry

Note: Since lowercase keystrokes now attempt to match the next entry, only uppercase alphabetic commands are available. The exception is that for users of the roguelike keyset, the usual up/down keys <color:keypress>k and <color:keypress>j will scroll up and down, even at the cost of not matching an entry.

Note: Filter toggles on this screen are remembered for the current game session.

Note: If <color:keyword>quick_messages is enabled, then an unhandled keystroke will dismiss the object list.

Usage

Once loot starts dropping everywhere, the object list is your best tool for seeing what you missed; and it also works well together with Object Detection and especially Clairvoyance. Since objects are sorted primarily by whether they are wanted by the Mogaminator, and secondarily by their estimated value, the most interesting objects are easy to spot even if the list is extremely long. Travelling to Objects

You may travel to the currently selected object in the object list by pressing J or (, the same keys used to resume an interrupted travel. (In the object list, both keys work equally regardless of your keyset.) Be careful when travelling across the level, though; you might travel into a horde of demons who only disturb you when it's too late. Travelling to remote targets is best used if you know the level is mostly empty; while it can be used in other situations, exercise caution and make sure you have <color:keyword>check_abort (see ) on.

Note that you can quickly select an item in the object list by pressing the first significant letter in its description. For example, to select the Black Market, simply press <color:keypress>b. Subwindow

You may set up the Object List as a subwindow to have it continuously displayed; although additional functionality such as travelling to objects or inspecting objects will not be available through the subwindow, it is still a handy way to see what you're missing and where the stairs and entrances are. See for details on setting up subwindows.

Shopping

Press for the &lt;color:keyword&gt;Quick Reference andfor details on shopping.

Each town on the surface contains numerous shops where you may purchase supplies or sell unwanted objects. Each shop specializes in a certain class of items: The Weapon Smiths sells weapons (melee and missile) while the Armory sells armor; the Alchemist sells potions and scrolls while the General Store sells basic utilities such as food, lanterns and oil. Each town also has a Black Market where you may, for an exorbitant price, purchase items normally found only in the dungeon.

Your First Shopping Spree

When you enter a shop, you will see a screen describing the shop's owner and the items available for purchase:

Vengella the Cruel (Half-Troll) Armory (15000)

[R] Reserve Item [S] Shuffle Stock [B] Buy Everything

A quick list of available commands is displayed on the bottom of the screen. Simply choose the appropriate command and follow the instructions. Use <color:keypress>Page Up and <color:keypress>Page Down if the shop inventory extends to multiple pages.

Press <color:keypress>u or <color:keypress>U to toggle hiding items your Mogaminator rules classify as Unwanted; while the filter is on the footer entry turns red and reads <color:keypress>Show Unwanted. The footer shows how many listed rows are affected (one per stack), and the count updates as the store contents change. If the Mogaminator is disabled, <color:keypress>u explains how to activate it first.

Every store owner has access to limited funds, and will only pay so much for items that you sell; this amount is listed next to the store type on the top of the display.

Targetting

The targetting prompt offers many options, and two different modes: <color:keyword>monster-targetting mode and <color:keyword>free-targetting mode. If there are hostile monsters in line of sight, targetting begins in monster-targetting mode; the first target offered will be the nearest such monster, with other hostile monsters in line of sight as alternative targets. Use direction keys to cycle between monsters; <color:keypress>+ and <color:keypress>- also work, but are less intuitive. Turn on the <color:keyword>target_pet option () if you want this mode to allow non-hostile monsters as targets.

If you wish to target (or inspect) a square with no monster on it, press <color:keypress>p or <color:keypress>o, switching to free-targetting mode where direction keys simply move the cursor. (This mode is automatically entered if no hostile monsters are in line of sight.) <color:keypress>o and <color:keypress>p are identical except in one respect: pressing <color:keypress>p (which stands for <color:keyword>player) moves the cursor to your own location, while pressing <color:keypress>o (which stands for <color:keyword>offset) does not.

At any time, press <color:keypress>5, <color:keypress>t or <color:keypress>. to accept the current target (and exit targetting mode), <color:keypress>q or <color:keypress>ESC to exit targetting mode without selecting a target, <color:keypress>r to recall lore about a monster on the target square, <color:keypress>x to see all items on the target square (including stolen or picked-up items carried by monsters, but excluding normal monster item drops), and <color:keypress>( to select a square as a travel target. In the original keyset, <color:keypress>J and <color:keypress>j also work as travel keys and are equivalent with <color:keypress>(.

If a visible or telepathically detected monster is standing on top of something you want to inspect, you can temporarily hide monster glyphs while looking around. In the original keyset, press <color:keypress>^L to enter this look-under mode. From the travel cursor, press <color:keypress>x to enter it in either keyset. This mode stays in free-targetting, lets <color:keypress>5, <color:keypress>t and <color:keypress>. select the current square even if occupied, and restores monster display when you leave it.

Users of the roguelike keyset have a bonus option in free-targetting mode: they can press <color:keypress>Shift+DIR to move the cursor many squares at a time.

Precision Targetting

When you cast a spell or fire a missile at a target location, the path chosen is the <color:keyword>direct path towards that location, which may or may not be the path you want. Sometimes, by clever choice of a side location as your target, you may be able to aim at squares not directly in line of sight:

Position: an unknown grid [q,t,p,m,x,j,+,-,?,<dir>]

##........#.... #%%####

#........\...... #

%.......}{\@.... #

%#%..........*.... #

## ........*... ... #

# ......*... .d. #

# ..(.#*. .#####

# .##* T #

# ^ #####* ##########

## # #* '

# # ##* ############

# # #* ###

# # ##* ##

## # # * #

# # ##* #

######### #*#########

Notice that bright-red *? There's a dragon on that square I cannot target directly; but I managed to include that square in my spell's path by using <color:keypress>p to target a location on the southern edge of the map.

Note that bolt spells always stop at the first monster in the spell's path, but beam and breath spells affect all squares in their paths, and ball spells can reach the target square by flying over monsters' heads if necessary.

Location Targets vs Monster Targets

When selecting a target, you may target either a <color:keyword>monster or a <color:keyword>location. This is an important difference: if you target a monster, the target will move when the monster moves; but if you target a location, the target remains stationary, even if the location had a monster in it.

If you bypass targetting mode you can also target a <color:keyword>compass direction, which for this purpose is always equivalent to targetting a <color:keyword>location, even if there was an obvious monster in the direction indicated. So watch out if there's a monster due west of you, you fire west and then spam <color:keypress>n (or <color:keypress>X in the roguelike keyset) to repeat: this will work beautifully as long as the monster remains due west, but as soon as it moves north or south you will need to retarget, something you would not have needed to do had you selected the monster as your target.

Quick Summary

<color:keypress>DIR Move to square or monster in direction indicated

<color:keypress>+ Move to more distant monster

<color:keypress>- Move to less distant monster

<color:keypress>( j J Select travel target (exit and travel if not aiming)

<color:keypress>m Enter monster-targetting mode

<color:keypress>p Enter free-targetting mode (move cursor to player)

<color:keypress>o Enter free-targetting mode (keep cursor location)

<color:keypress>r Recall monster lore

<color:keypress>x Cycle between items on target square

<color:keypress>? Display this help topic

Cornucopia Banking and Insurance Services - Terms and Conditions

Cornucopia of Anambar ("Cornucopia") is your only option for personal banking, highly interesting loans and item insurance. By using any Cornucopia product or service, such as the Cornucopia Banking and Insurance Services ("Services") or the Cornucopia Official Help File ("Terms" or "Terms and Conditions"), you signify your agreement to all terms and conditions set out herein, which may be revised by Cornucopia or by the FrogComposband Maintainer (the "Maintainer") from time to time without explicit notice.

Deposit Accounts

As a Cornucopia customer, you (the "Customer") are entitled to open one (1) personal deposit account ("Account") at any Cornucopia office. Every time you deposit money in your Account, you will be charged a transaction fee of 500 gold pieces (or 0.02 percent of the money being deposited, whichever is higher), to be paid immediately. Your deposits will accumulate compound interest at a rate of 0.01 percent per diem, added to your Account every midnight. You may withdraw money from your Account at any time at any Cornucopia office, without additional transaction fees.

Loans

Cornucopia offers loans to customers ("Loans") up to a total amount of 1,500 gold pieces, or twice your reforge limit (up to a maximum of one-tenth of your known career gross earnings), whichever is higher, the initial Loan not exceeding 300,000 gold pieces. Cornucopia charges compound interest on all Loans at a rate of 10 percent per diem, applying immediately upon request of the Loan, and subsequently every midnight. The Loan can be repaid, fully or in part, at any time at any Cornucopia office. Cornucopia values prompt repayment of loans, but there is no absolute deadline for repayment - we are happy to repossess your estate if necessary. However, in the case of a very large outstanding Loan (exceeding 400,000 gold pieces) not covered by deposits in your Account, Cornucopia reserves the right to refuse you all further Services, including but not limited to settlement of insurance claims and withdrawal of deposits, until such time as the Loan is reduced to no more than 300,000 gold pieces.

Insurance

Cornucopia offers two basic types of item insurance policy ("Policies"): insurance against disenchantment of the item ("Disenchantment Insurance"), and insurance against destruction of the item ("Destruction Insurance"), as further explained below. A single Policy can cover either one item, or in the case of Destruction Insurance, one pile of identical items. As a Cornucopia customer, you may have up to four (4) Policies at any given time, and replace any Policy that has become inactive with a new, active Policy.

<color:keyword>Disenchantment Insurance applies to a wearable item ("Equipment"), and can be bought by the Customer for any base value ("Value") of up to 2,000 gold pieces, or one-twentieth of the item's value, whichever is lower. If the insured Equipment is disenchanted for any reason, the Customer will be entitled to claim monetary recompense ("Compensation") according to the severity of the damage and the quality of the item. The amount of Compensation per unit of damage for each type of disenchantment, shown in units of half the Value, is displayed in the table below:

To Hit To Dam To AC Pval

Normal Weapon 1 2 3 2

Ego Weapon 2 4 6 20

Artifact Weapon 4 8 12 40

Normal Armour 3 6 1 2

Ego Armour 6 12 2 20

Artifact Armour 12 24 4 40

No Compensation shall be paid for any damages that can be easily repaired by the Customer. The following damages shall be considered easily repairable: any damage that can be repaired at the Fighters' Hall, at the time the damage is suffered; for users of the Craft realm, any damage that can be repaired with the Enchantment spell; for weaponsmiths, any damage that can be repaired by a level 50 weaponsmith.

<color:keyword>Destruction Insurance applies to an inventory item (Potion, Scroll, Staff or Wand), or to a pile of identical Scrolls or Potions. A Destruction Insurance Policy can cover an item in either or both of two ways: an identical item is provided to the Customer by Cornucopia ("Item Replacement"), or Compensation is paid for the destruction of the item ("Item Compensation").

An Item Compensation Policy ("Regular Plan") can be bought for a Value of one-third the insured item's value for Staves and Wands, or the full amount of the insured item's value for Scrolls and Potions. If the insured item is destroyed by an enemy attack while in the Customer's inventory, the Customer is entitled to claim Compensation up to four times the Value for Staves and Wands, or two times the Value for Scrolls and Potions.

An Item Replacement Policy ("Replacement Plan") can be bought for fifteen times the insured item's value, or thirty times the insured item's value in case of ego items, for Staves and Wands only. If the item so insured is destroyed, an identical item will be provided to the Customer at a Cornucopia office. The original Replacement Plan will not apply to the copy.

All Destruction Insurance Policies only apply to items in the Customer's equipment or inventory, damaged or destroyed by enemy attacks. No Policies cover theft, items dropped on the dungeon floor, lost accidentally, consumed, or destroyed or made unavailable to the Customer in any other additional way. Disenchantment Insurance Policies only cover damage from disenchantment, not similar damage resulting from other sources such as acid attacks. Unlike some insurance companies, however, we do cover acts of God.

You agree not to deliberately seek situations in which an insured item is likely to be disenchanted or destroyed.

Exposure Limits

Cornucopia's insurance exposure limit with respect to you (the "Limit") is equal to one percent of your lifetime gold acquired, never being less than 5,000 gold pieces, and never being more than 50,000 gold pieces. The lifetime monetary losses of Cornucopia, resulting from Policies with Compensation claimed by you, and excluding all money used to buy Item Replacement policies and all monetary transactions not involving any Policy, shall never exceed the Limit. Any Compensation claimed by you in excess of the Limit shall be forfeited to and kept by Cornucopia, and shall not be considered owed to you. Cornucopia shall warn you when settling a claim would result in the Limit being exceeded.

The Limits were set up in response to the substantial losses incurred by Cornucopia in its dealings with the adventurer Implorington III ("That Two-Faced Bastard"), later determined to have been the result of insurance fraud, and we regret their necessity.
